value.overview: The Slate-colored Grosbeak (Saltator grossus) is a large, strong-billed tanager of humid tropical forests. It is usually secretive, often remaining within dense vegetation while giving distinctive calls. The species occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and into northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it is mainly associated with humid Caribbean-slope forests and foothill habitats, where it is generally uncommon and localized rather than widespread in open country.
value.classification: The Slate-colored Grosbeak belongs to the tanager family Thraupidae and the genus Saltator. It is not a true finch or grosbeak, despite its common name.
value.identification: This is a bulky saltator with a heavy, reddish to orange-red bill, dark slate-gray upperparts, and contrasting darker markings around the face and throat. The underparts are generally paler gray, with variation in the strength of the throat and breast pattern. Its large bill and deep-bodied shape help separate it from smaller saltators. It is more often detected by its loud, ringing vocalizations than by prolonged views in dense forest.
value.rangeHabitat: The Slate-colored Grosbeak ranges from southern Mexico through Central America to parts of northern and western South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs primarily on the humid Caribbean slope, especially in lowland and foothill forest, forest edges, second growth, and other well-vegetated areas. It is generally found from the lowlands into the foothills, but records are local and it is not an evenly distributed species across the country. It favors dense vegetation and forest with substantial cover.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica, the Slate-colored Grosbeak is considered a resident species rather than a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur in response to food availability or seasonal conditions, but there is no well-established pattern of broad seasonal migration.
value.breeding: The breeding biology of the Slate-colored Grosbeak is incompletely documented across much of its range. Like related saltators, it is believed to nest in dense vegetation, placing a cup-shaped nest in shrubs or low trees. Breeding activity is likely seasonal and may vary geographically with rainfall. Territorial calls and pair behavior are important signs during the breeding period, but detailed information on clutch size, incubation, and parental care remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on fruits, berries, and seeds, and it may also take insects and other small invertebrates, particularly when feeding young. Its powerful bill is well suited to handling hard or large food items. It usually forages within foliage and tangled vegetation, often alone or in pairs, and may visit fruiting plants along forest edges or in mature second growth.
value.behavior: Slate-colored Grosbeaks are generally wary and less conspicuous than many other tanagers. They spend much of their time in dense vegetation, moving deliberately while searching for food. Pairs or small family groups may defend territories with loud, repeated calls. The species can remain hidden even when calling nearby, so careful listening is often the best way to locate it. It may join mixed-species feeding groups occasionally, but it is not strongly flock-dependent.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not known with confidence. The species has a broad distribution, but local populations may be affected by the loss and fragmentation of humid forest.
